Source: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability (Princeton, ICML 2026)
What it says: Separates pass@k (can it ever succeed) from pass^k (does it succeed every time); finds reliability barely improved in 24 months despite big capability gains.
How it moved this feature: Gave the exact idea and vocabulary for this feature and established the problem it solves.

What it says: Proves a single 'which answer wins' score can look identical whether the real success rate is 90% or 20%.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent confirmation that one number hides reliability, which strengthened the case.

What it says: All 8 major agent benchmarks audited were exploitable; 6 reached ~100% scores without genuinely solving anything.
How it moved this feature: Proved that scores are frequently mis-attributed, which is exactly what showing where a run failed prevents.

What it says: An independent audit of 15 benchmarks found roughly 67% of runs inflated by shortcuts rather than real skill.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent proof of the same problem, strengthening the case for attribution.

What it says: Shows agents sometimes exploit stored outcome information instead of actually solving the task.
How it moved this feature: Reinforces the need to attribute a result to the agent versus the environment.

What it says: Builds a 7-category taxonomy of why agents fail across a multi-step task.
How it moved this feature: A concrete reference for how we might categorize and label failures in the UI.

What it says: Argues ranking agents on accuracy alone is misleading and shows accuracy against cost as a frontier instead.
How it moved this feature: The reference design behind always showing a cost or reliability axis next to the score.

What it says: Maintainers had to declare scores non-comparable across a version after fixing a grading bug.
How it moved this feature: A real, dated example of why comparisons need guardrails.

What it says: Agents often continue on impossible tasks, with false-continue rates up to 74% across nine models.
How it moved this feature: Establishes the problem; a single source, which is why this stays low-confidence for now.

Source: The Judge in the Mirror (self-preference pilot)
What it says: A pilot found LLM judges rated their own model family about 0.14 higher on a normalized index.
How it moved this feature: The first signal that LLM judges are biased toward their own family.

Source: LLMs Trust Their Own: Identity-Dependent Conformity
What it says: Across 12 models and 9 tasks, judges favored their own family or identity regardless of the correct answer.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent proof, which promoted the underlying hypothesis and moved this feature from the bottom to the top of the list.

What it says: Has a three-tier approval system, but its docs never say whether a confirmation names the specific consequence of the action.
How it moved this feature: Shows that what to show when asking for approval is an unsolved gap, an opportunity.

What it says: Runs ~3M sandboxes a day with stateful pause/resume and checkpoint/branch, but does no verification or grading.
How it moved this feature: Proves the backend capability exists at scale; our opportunity is to make that lifecycle legible in the product.

What it says: Stateful, freely-mutable worlds at scale prompted the question of how imported or edited worlds get graded.
How it moved this feature: Provided the context that sparked this idea.

What it says: Realism and verifiability are not opposed; the real constraint is that any state you grade against needs a known correct answer.
How it moved this feature: Sharpened the feature to its core: capture ground truth for worlds we did not mint.
